title: Branching Basics
description: Creating and managing branches in Git

content.overview: Branches in Git allow you to diverge from the main line of development and work on features or fixes independently. In this module, you'll learn how to create, switch between, and manage branches in Git.

steps.title: What are Branches?
steps.content: Branches in Git are lightweight movable pointers to commits. They allow you to work on different features or fixes in isolation without affecting the main codebase. The default branch in Git is called 'master' or 'main'.

steps.title: Viewing Branches
steps.content: You can view all branches in your repository using the `git branch` command. The current branch is marked with an asterisk (*).

behindTheCommand.title: How Git Tracks Branches
behindTheCommand.content: Git stores branch information in the `.git/refs/heads/` directory. Each branch is a file containing the commit hash that the branch points to. When you run `git branch`, Git reads these files to display the branch names.

steps.title: Creating a New Branch
steps.content: You can create a new branch using the `git branch` command followed by the branch name. This creates a new pointer to the current commit but doesn't switch to the new branch.

fileChanges.description: Git creates a new file for the branch in the .git/refs/heads/ directory

behindTheCommand.title: What Happens When Creating a Branch
behindTheCommand.content: When you create a new branch, Git simply creates a new file in the `.git/refs/heads/` directory with the branch name. This file contains the SHA-1 hash of the commit that the branch points to. Initially, this is the same commit that your current branch points to. No changes are made to your working directory or the staging area.

steps.title: Switching Branches
steps.content: To switch to a different branch, use the `git checkout` command followed by the branch name. This updates your working directory to match the state of the branch.

behindTheCommand.title: What Happens During Checkout
behindTheCommand.content:
When you run `git checkout`, Git performs several operations:

1. Updates the HEAD pointer to point to the specified branch
2. Updates the index (staging area) to match the target branch
3. Updates the working directory to match the target branch

This means files in your working directory may change, be added, or be removed to match the state of the branch you're switching to.

steps.title: Creating and Switching in One Command
steps.content: You can create a new branch and switch to it in one command using `git checkout -b`.

commands.description: Switch back to the main branch
Create and switch to a new branch named 'new-feature'

behindTheCommand.title: Combining Branch Creation and Checkout
behindTheCommand.content:
The `git checkout -b` command is a convenience shortcut that combines two operations:

1. `git branch <branch-name>` - Creates a new branch pointing to the current commit
2. `git checkout <branch-name>` - Switches to the newly created branch

This is one of Git's most commonly used commands when starting work on a new feature or bugfix. It allows you to quickly create an isolated environment for your changes.

steps.title: Making Changes on a Branch
steps.content: Once you're on a branch, you can make changes, commit them, and push them to a remote repository without affecting other branches.

commands.description: Create a new file for the feature

commands.expectedOutput:
[new-feature (root-commit) 1234abc] Add new feature
 1 file changed, 1 insertion(+)
 create mode 100644 feature.txt

behindTheCommand.title: Branch Divergence
behindTheCommand.content:
When you make commits on a branch, that branch's pointer moves forward to the new commit, while other branches remain pointing to their respective commits. This is how Git allows parallel development streams.

Each branch can evolve independently, with its own set of changes. Later, these changes can be combined through merging or rebasing.

steps.title: Viewing Branch History
steps.content: You can view the commit history of a branch using the `git log` command.

commands.description: View a compact history of the current branch
commands.expectedOutput:
1234abc (HEAD -> new-feature) Add new feature
5678def (main, feature) Initial commit

behindTheCommand.title: Commit History and Branch Pointers
behindTheCommand.content:
The `git log` command shows the commit history starting from the current HEAD and working backward through parent commits. When you include the `--oneline` flag, Git shows a compact view with just the commit hash and message.

The output also shows branch pointers in parentheses, indicating which branches point to which commits. This helps you visualize the current state of your repository's branches.
